source.publication: 2025 MI-1040 Forms and Instructions (includes Form 4884 instructions)
source.section: Schedule 1 line 26 (PDF page 17: older spouse born January 1, 1953 through January 1, 1959 and 67 by December 31, 2025; up to 40,000 joint, reduced by exemptions on lines 9a and 9d and taxable Social Security); Worksheet 2 lines 1-11 (PDF page 18); MI-1040 lines 9a, 10, 13-17 (PDF page 10 Line 9a, Line 10, Line 17; PDF page 11 example: line 14 income subject to tax less line 15 exemptions = line 16 taxable income)

worked: Federal AGI = spouse 2 wages 30,000.00 + interest 20,000.00 + dividends 10,000.00 + taxable Social Security 20,400.00 (85% of 24,000.00) = 80,400.00. Federal taxable income = 80,400.00 - federal standard deduction (31,500 + 2 x 1,600 age 65 or older = 34,700.00) = 45,700.00; given, not tested; the federal senior deduction is ignored. Michigan (older spouse born 1956, past 67; no SSA-exempt benefits, so Tier 3): Schedule 1 line 14 Social Security 20,400.00. Worksheet 2: line 1 40,000.00; line 2 0.00; line 3 40,000.00; lines 4-6 0.00; line 7 40,000.00; line 8 taxable Social Security 20,400.00. As the projection does it (approximation: exemptions not subtracted, line 9 left out): Tier 3 = 40,000.00 - 20,400.00 = 19,600.00, less than the 60,000.00 of wages, interest and dividends; subtractions 40,000.00; line 14 = 80,400.00 - 40,000.00 = 40,400.00; exemptions 11,600.00; line 16 = 28,800.00. MI-1040 line 17 tax = 28,800.00 x 0.0425 = 1,224.00. No credits; state income tax 1,224.00. The form itself also subtracts line 9 exemptions 11,600.00 on Worksheet 2 line 9: line 10 = 20,400.00 + 11,600.00 = 32,000.00; line 11 Tier 3 = 8,000.00; taxable income 40,400.00; tax 1,717.00, which is 493.00 more (4.25% x 11,600.00), the size the approximation states. No pensions, so Worksheet 3.3 gives 0.00 and Tier 3 is the better choice either way.
accepted_approximations: The Tier 3 deduction is also reduced by exemptions claimed (MI-1040 lines 9a and 9d); not modelled.
